questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: classify the main kinds of regime change
questions.stem: Analysts sort regime change into several kinds. Which description matches a move from authoritarian rule to democracy reached through an agreement between the outgoing rulers and their opponents?

options.text: A negotiated transition, in which the outgoing rulers and the opposition accept a deal
A collapse, in which the old regime falls apart before any deal is concluded
options.misconception: treats the absence of fighting as proof that no agreement existed

options.text: A rupture, in which the old authorities are removed by force before any ballot is held
options.misconception: confuses any negotiated route with one driven by the military

options.text: A restoration, in which a previous ruler is returned to office by the new order
options.misconception: reads the return of a former leader as the same event as a change of regime

questions.explanation: The three kinds differ in who drives the change and what the old rulers get out of it. In a negotiated transition the rulers who are leaving agree to the terms, so the sequence is a bargain rather than a collapse or an armed removal. A collapse is what analysts call the situation where the old regime disintegrates under strain before any such agreement is reached, so the absence of visible violence proves nothing about the character of the change. A rupture involves removing the old authorities by force, and a restoration is the return of a former leader, which is a different event again.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rulers who were leaving had a say in the terms.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain a legitimation crisis as a cause of breakdown
questions.stem: One recurring cause of authoritarian breakdown is described as a legitimation crisis. What is happening when a government suffers from that condition?

options.text: Those it governs largely cease to accept that it has the right to rule them
The government can no longer pay the salaries of its own security services
options.misconception: confuses a loss of popular acceptance with a shortage of money

options.text: Leading members of the ruling party dispute who should succeed an ageing leader
options.misconception: reduces a crisis of legitimacy to a dispute about one office

options.text: The price of the main export falls far enough to shrink the state budget
options.misconception: substitutes an economic shock for the loss of accepted right to rule

questions.explanation: Legitimation is the belief that a government is entitled to govern, and a crisis of it means that belief has collapsed among the population rather than among its own members. That is why economic strain and elite argument are related problems but not the same thing: a falling export price weakens the government's capacity and can precipitate the political crisis, yet a government can also face a legitimation crisis while the economy is doing well, if the public no longer accepts its claim. A shortfall in the security payroll is a funding problem, and a succession dispute concerns a single office, neither of which touches acceptance of the regime as such.
questions.hint: Ask who has stopped believing the government is entitled to govern them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a pacted from a consolidated democracy
questions.stem: A democracy produced by an explicit bargain between former opponents is called pacted; one that has survived the alternation of power is called consolidated. What separates the two?

options.text: Whether the new order has been tested by losing power and then taking it back
Whether the constitution was drafted before or after the first election was held
options.misconception: dates the label to the sequence of texts and ballots

options.text: Whether seats are allocated in proportion to votes or through single districts
options.misconception: reads the label as a statement about the electoral formula in use

options.text: Whether a two-party system or a multi-party system emerged after the change
options.misconception: fixes the label on the number of parties rather than on how the order has held

questions.explanation: The distinction turns on evidence, not on the circumstances of the founding moment. Every transitional democracy begins with some kind of agreement, so the pact describes how the order began, while consolidation describes what has since happened to it: that the losers of an election handed over, and then won a later one and handed back. A constitution's date and the electoral formula are settled at the founding moment and say nothing about durability, and the same bargain can produce a two-party order or a multi-party one without changing its standing. So the test is whether power has actually changed hands and been returned.
questions.hint: Ask what has happened to the winners and losers since the deal was made.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: read a transition chronology for evidence of consolidation

stimulus.body: Chronology of a transition, written for this question. In month 1 a constituent assembly is elected by a system allocating seats in proportion to votes. In month 4 the assembly adopts a constitution providing that the assembly's term cannot be shortened and that the courts may review executive acts. In month 7 the assembly confirms that the outgoing rulers may stand for office and grants them amnesty for acts before the reform. In month 10 a first election is held and the party that had opposed the outgoing rulers wins a majority. In month 30 that government loses the following election and transfers power without force. In month 84 the party that won in month 10 wins again.

questions.stem: An extract sets out the chronology of a transition: a proportional constituent assembly at month 1, a constitution guaranteeing a fixed term and judicial review of executive acts at month 4, an amnesty and eligibility for the outgoing rulers at month 7, a first election the former opposition wins at month 10, a change of government without force at month 30, and a repeat win for the same party at month 84. Which feature of that chronology is the evidence for consolidation?

options.text: Power changed hands at an election and was handed back without force
A constitution fixing the assembly's term and court review came first
options.misconception: treats the founding texts as the test of how well the order has held

options.text: The outgoing rulers were granted amnesty and allowed to stand again
options.misconception: reads a clause protecting the departing side as proof of durability

options.text: The first election allocated seats in proportion to the votes cast
options.misconception: mistakes an electoral formula in the founding month for later evidence

questions.explanation: Consolidation is established by the losers accepting defeat and later returning to power, so the entries at month 30 and month 84 are the ones that bear on it. The month 30 entry shows an incumbent handing over office after losing, which is the check that a pact alone cannot supply, and the month 84 entry shows the same party winning again, so the arrangement survives contact with a second contest. The constitution, the amnesty and the proportional first ballot are all features of how the order was founded; they are part of the settlement but none of them demonstrates that the settlement has held. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask which entry shows the losing side actually obeying the result.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify an instance of coup-proofing
questions.stem: Authoritarian incumbents adopt measures intended to reduce the risk of being overthrown by their own armed forces, a set of practices known as coup-proofing. Which measure fits that category?

options.text: Placing military appointments under a civilian command structure loyal to the incumbent
Rotating senior officers each year so that none of them builds a following
options.misconception: confuses a policy designed to prevent a coup with one designed to cause one

options.text: Publishing the armed forces' internal correspondence in an open government gazette
options.misconception: invents a transparency measure as though it removed the danger of a coup

options.text: Holding joint exercises with the armed forces of a neighbouring state
options.misconception: treats foreign cooperation as a way of disarming the domestic military

questions.explanation: Coup-proofing works on the logic that a government is vulnerable to a coup when the armed forces can act on their own initiative, so the standard measures all reduce that autonomy. Subordinating appointments to a civilian command loyal to the incumbent means the chain of promotion no longer runs through the generals alone, and related measures do the same by splitting command, staggering terms and clearing potentially disloyal officers. Rotating officers is a plausible administrative practice but it is not what the term denotes, and transparency rules and foreign exercises have no bearing on who may remove a government. So the answer is A.
questions.hint: Ask which measure reduces the armed forces' power to act on their own.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why dividing the military defeats a coup
questions.stem: One coup-proofing measure is to split the armed forces into rival units placed under different commanders. Why is that effective at deterring a takeover?

options.text: A takeover needs unified control of the troops, which a rivalry between units denies
Rival units can be ordered to arrest each other's senior commanders
options.misconception: invents a use for the rivalry that no coup-proofing scheme relies on

options.text: The rivalry raises what soldiers must be paid, so the ranks grow harder to buy
options.misconception: substitutes a change in pay for a change in command structure

options.text: Rival units can be counted against one another in any vote the legislature takes
options.misconception: moves a command arrangement into the counting of votes in a chamber

questions.explanation: A coup succeeds only if the men with the guns act together, so the most reliable way to prevent it is to ensure they cannot. Dividing the military into units with separate chains of command leaves no single person able to command the whole force at once, and any plotter has to win over several rival commands rather than one. The other three answers attach a function to the arrangement that it does not serve: no scheme relies on units arresting each other, and neither pay nor the legislature's arithmetic is what the division is for. What matters is the absence of unified control, which is exactly why the measure appears in this category.
questions.hint: Ask what a conspirator must be able to do before a takeover can succeed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Coalition arithmetic at the point of transition
questions.learningObjective: apply majority arithmetic to a legislature's composition
questions.stem: A legislature of 200 seats contains three blocs holding 96, 61 and 43 seats. A president is to be chosen by the legislature itself. What follows from these numbers?

options.text: A majority of 101 is needed, so the 96-seat bloc cannot elect anyone alone
A majority of 100 is needed, so the 96-seat bloc needs only five more votes
options.misconception: takes half the chamber as the threshold and forgets the extra member

options.text: A majority of 96 is needed, so the largest bloc is already in control
options.misconception: reads the largest bloc's seat count as though it were a threshold

options.text: A two-thirds majority of 134 is needed, which no pair of blocs can muster
options.misconception: claims no pair can reach a total that the two largest blocs comfortably exceed

questions.explanation: A bare majority of a full chamber is half the members plus one, so 200 seats require 101 votes. The largest bloc's 96 seats fall five short, which is why it must reach another bloc, and the two largest together hold 157, leaving exactly the 43 seats of the third, so the figures are internally consistent. Treating 100 as the threshold drops the extra member and would hand the largest bloc a working majority it does not have, while 96 is simply the size of a bloc rather than a rule. Two thirds of 200 is 134, and 157 clears it, so the claim that no pair can manage it is false.
questions.hint: A majority of a full chamber is half the members plus one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: select the measures that entrench an incumbent
questions.stem: Which of the following are used by authoritarian incumbents to make their own removal harder? Select all that apply.

options.text: Staggering the terms of the offices that appoint and dismiss the security services
Raising the legislative threshold for reversing an earlier decree
Redrawing constituency boundaries shortly before the scheduled election
options.misconception: confuses a tactic aimed at seats with a device that protects the office

options.text: Requiring judicial approval of the government's legislative programme
options.misconception: mistakes judicial oversight for a device that protects the holder of office

options.text: Giving judges fixed terms that expire well after the incumbent's own

questions.explanation: The three correct measures all raise the cost of removing the incumbent. Staggering the terms of the offices that control the security services means no single successor inherits the whole apparatus, so an incoming government cannot be sure of the chain of command. A raised threshold for reversing a decree makes the incumbent's own acts difficult to undo. Judicial terms outlasting the incumbent mean the courts he appoints remain in place after he leaves, which is why it belongs here. Redrawing boundaries is an electoral tactic rather than a protection of the office, and requiring judicial approval of a legislative programme limits the government instead of securing it.
questions.hint: Ask, for each measure, whether the incumbent benefits or is constrained by it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain the strategic effect of boundary manipulation
questions.stem: Before an election, an incumbent's government redraws constituencies so that its supporters are packed densely into a smaller number of districts. What is the strategic effect of that move?

options.text: Its support is converted into seats more efficiently, so a larger majority becomes likely
Its support is spread evenly, which turns every district into a genuine contest
options.misconception: expects a packing operation to disperse votes rather than concentrate them

options.text: Fewer votes in total are needed to reach the same number of seats
options.misconception: claims a reduction in the votes required where the map changes the mapping

options.text: Opposition voters are struck from the electoral roll in greater numbers
options.misconception: substitutes a change to the register for a change to the map

questions.explanation: Packing supporters into few districts wastes their numerical strength in districts they win by huge margins, while the opposition is spread thinly and loses districts it would have carried had they been combined. The total seat count is fixed, so the gain has to come from the conversion of votes rather than from any reduction in the votes needed. Boundary manipulation does not touch the electoral roll, which is why the last answer describes a different practice. And the effect of packing is to concentrate rather than disperse, which is the opposite of what the second answer claims.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the votes of supporters who are spread across many districts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Performance as a source of legitimation
questions.learningObjective: identify material performance as a mode of legitimation
questions.stem: An authoritarian government raises pensions and improves a city's public transport, while elections stay uncompetitive and the legislature remains weak. What is the most likely mechanism at work?

options.text: Material performance is offered in place of the political consent an election would give
Power is being shared with those who benefit, which is what representation means
options.misconception: recasts the distribution of benefits as a sharing of formal authority

options.text: A democratic mandate is being satisfied by the means the voters would have chosen
options.misconception: treats unelected delivery as though it carried a popular mandate

options.text: The cost of opposition is being reduced, making campaigns easier to organise
options.misconception: describes a liberalising effect that the scenario explicitly excludes

questions.explanation: A government that cannot win consent at the ballot box can seek it through delivery instead, and the mechanism is substitution: public improvements stand in for the legitimacy an election would confer. That is why the scenario pairs tangible gains with an uncompetitive ballot and a weak legislature, since without those the improvements would be read as ordinary government rather than as a substitute. Nothing in the case distributes authority, which is what representation means, and improving a service does not satisfy a mandate nobody was given. Nor does it make organising opposition easier, since the scenario states the contest remains closed.
questions.hint: Ask what the improvements are doing in place of the thing the ballot does not provide.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state what the third wave label denotes
questions.stem: Comparative politics uses the phrase third wave for a pattern of regime change observed across many countries. What does the label refer to?

options.text: A set of countries that moved from authoritarian rule towards democracy from the mid-1970s
The third round of elections held in one country after its regime changed
options.misconception: reads a cross-country pattern as repeated ballots inside a single state

options.text: A third rank of regimes placed below both democracies and authoritarian states
options.misconception: confuses a chronological grouping with a place in a ranking of regime types

options.text: A third stage of national development that every democracy must pass through
options.misconception: turns a group of events into a compulsory sequence of development

questions.explanation: The label is chronological and plural: it names a cluster of transitions that many countries underwent over roughly the same period, beginning in the mid-1970s, and the term is borrowed from a much older description of waves of change in human affairs. Its whole point is to group separate national events into one pattern, which is why reading it as a third election inside one country loses the cross-country dimension, and why treating it as a third rank of regime type confuses when with where a state sits. Nor does it describe a stage every democracy must pass through, since countries reach democracy by very different routes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the label is naming a time period across many countries or a stage within one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a stalemate in a transitional legislature
questions.stem: A transition stalls. The government and its opponents each hold exactly half the legislature, elections recur on schedule, and almost nothing passes. What is the central difficulty?

options.text: Neither side can command a majority, so the new rules are never put to a real test
The electoral system is too finely balanced, since every contest ends in an exact tie
options.misconception: attributes a recurring stalemate to a single drawn election

options.text: The armed forces refuse to recognise any of the parties taking part in the contests
options.misconception: invents a military refusal that the scenario does not report

options.text: The electorate is too small, so each individual vote carries undue weight
options.misconception: shifts attention to district size while the balance is described as exact

questions.explanation: Stalemate happens when the arithmetic of the chamber leaves no side able to govern, so the new institutions are never exercised by anyone with a mandate to use them. That is the structural problem, and it is what makes the situation dangerous for consolidation: rules that have never governed anything have not been shown to work. The distractors each invent a feature the scenario does not report, since it describes recurring elections, no military refusal and an exact balance of seats rather than a small electorate. Nothing about the size of the electorate explains why no majority forms.
questions.hint: Ask why no government in this legislature can pass anything on its own votes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: interpret a dataset of coup attempts

stimulus.body: Extract from a regional study, written for this question. Between 1990 and 2020 the study records forty attempted coups across the countries surveyed. Seven attempts failed: in five the commanding officer declined to act, and in two civilian forces repelled the attackers. Thirty-three attempts succeeded in installing a new government. In twenty-two of those thirty-three successful cases the incoming government later held elections within three years.

questions.stem: An extract from a regional study records that between 1990 and 2020 there were forty attempted coups across the countries surveyed; seven failed, five because the commanding officer declined to act and two because civilian forces repelled the attackers; thirty-three succeeded in installing a new government; and in twenty-two of those thirty-three the incoming government later held elections within three years. Which statement about those countries does the extract support?

options.text: Most attempts succeeded, and most of the successes were followed by elections
Under one attempt in ten failed, so a military refusal to act was uncommon
options.misconception: reports a success rate for failures that the counts do not produce

options.text: Because elections usually followed, the ballot was the normal route to power
options.misconception: inverts the frequency of elections after success into elections before it

options.text: Civilian forces repelled every attempt that failed, so civilian defence was decisive
options.misconception: overstates the two civilian successes to cover all seven failures

questions.explanation: Thirty-three of forty attempts succeeded, which is 82.5 percent, and twenty-two of those thirty-three is about 66.7 percent, so both halves of the answer follow from the counts. The first statement is the only one the arithmetic supports. Under one attempt in ten would mean fewer than four failures and the study reports seven, which is 17.5 percent, so the second statement understates failure and overstates the rarity of refusal. Elections following a takeover are not evidence that the ballot was the normal route, and of the seven failures only two were repelled by civilians, so the fourth statement inflates a minority case into a general one.
questions.hint: Compare the successes with the attempts, then the elections with the successes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: state the limits of conditional external support
questions.stem: External actors sometimes condition recognition or development aid on a government holding elections. What is the chief limitation of that form of leverage?

options.text: The promise depends on donors being prepared to withdraw it once the deadline passes
Elections are the one thing an authoritarian government cannot afford to allow
options.misconception: asserts a blanket impossibility where the leverage is precisely about elections

options.text: Donors have no way to tell whether a promised election is genuinely competitive
options.misconception: overstates the monitoring problem where elections can be observed and judged

options.text: Development aid usually rises after a transition instead of triggering one
options.misconception: describes the timing of aid flows rather than the limits of conditionality

questions.explanation: Conditionality works through a threat of withdrawal, and a threat is only as credible as the willingness to carry it out. The commonest weakness is that donors weigh the political cost of withdrawing against the cost of continuing to support a government that has not held the promised election, and if they routinely defer, the condition loses its force. Observers can and do assess whether an election was competitive, so the third answer describes a real difficulty without being the binding one. The remaining options either state an impossibility the leverage exists to circumvent or describe a trend in aid volumes, not the mechanism's reliability.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a conditional promise once the deadline passes without action.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the problem an exit guarantee addresses
questions.stem: In a negotiated transition, departing rulers are guaranteed personal immunity and a pension, and the outgoing security forces keep their ranks for a year. What problem does such a package chiefly address?

options.text: The fear that a side with nothing to lose will resist or plot a return to office
The absence of any written constitution to govern the months after the change
options.misconception: attaches the package to a constitutional gap it does not remedy

options.text: The shortage of officials willing to accept office in the new government
options.misconception: solves a recruitment problem the arrangement was never designed to meet

options.text: The risk that an electoral commission will be staffed by one party's allies
options.misconception: describes an administrative risk the guarantees leave entirely untouched

questions.explanation: The economics of a transition are about incentives on both sides. A departing elite that fears arrest or ruin has a strong reason to sabotage the settlement, and explicit immunity plus a pension removes that reason, while keeping the old security forces in place for a year buys the new government time to build its own. This is why the package is described as an exit guarantee: it pays for the departing side's acceptance rather than for any institutional deficiency. It does not supply a constitution, recruit officials for the new government or change who staffs an electoral commission, so the remaining options misattach the arrangement to problems it was not built for.
questions.hint: Ask what a departing ruler's incentive to obstruct the change would be without such a promise.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish gradual erosion from a takeover by force
questions.stem: Two routes by which a democracy can end are often contrasted. How does gradual erosion differ from a takeover by force?

options.text: It keeps the formal rules standing while removing the conditions for real competition
It proceeds faster, because no legislative majority is needed to begin it
options.misconception: claims a procedural speed that belongs to the executive route

options.text: It always opens by suspending the constitution for a stated period
options.misconception: makes a suspension a necessary first step in a process that avoids it

options.text: It operates by written amendment rather than by executive action
options.misconception: confuses a route through the legislature with one that bypasses it

questions.explanation: Erosion works on the institutions while leaving their outward form intact, so a constitution, an election and a legislature all continue to exist and function formally, but the conditions that make them mean something are removed one at a time. A takeover by force abandons that subtlety and simply replaces the people in charge. That is why erosion is harder to answer: it is less visible, and it leaves an opposition with formal rights it cannot exercise. The other three answers attach features to erosion that belong to a different route, since a constitutional suspension and a legislative amendment both use the state's own legal machinery rather than avoiding it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the legal framework survives the change in this route.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of a transition to consolidation
questions.stem: Put these five stages in the order they typically follow when an authoritarian regime gives way to a democracy that has been tested by losing and regaining power.

options.text: A crisis of legitimacy unsettles the elite that had been managing the regime
Rulers and opponents settle a negotiated way for authority to change hands
A first election is held that the former opposition is able to win
The new government writes and then applies institutions that also bind it
Power passes to the opposition and later returns by election without force

questions.explanation: The order runs from cause to test. A legitimacy crisis has to come first, because it is what loosens the elite's grip and makes a bargain possible; without it there is no reason for anyone to negotiate. The bargain then supplies a method of transfer, and the first election is where that method is actually risked, since the former opposition must be able to win. Building institutions follows, because a government that intends to leave office cannot leave the state without rules, and the final stage is the test that distinguishes a settled order from one still resting on the original agreement. So the sequence is A, B, C, D, E.
questions.hint: Ask which stage supplies the reason for anyone to negotiate at all.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the condition that makes mobilisation decisive
questions.stem: Sustained street mobilisation is a common feature of political transitions. Which condition makes it decisive rather than merely disruptive?

options.text: It persists long enough to coordinate opposition and to make repression too costly
A single leader emerges who issues a programme the crowds will accept
options.misconception: substitutes personal leadership for the capacity of a movement to persist

options.text: It secures passage of a written constitution before talks with the government open
options.misconception: assigns a constitutional drafting task to a phase of public protest

options.text: It lowers turnout at elections, which forces a reform of the electoral system
options.misconception: claims a suppression of voting as the route to electoral reform

questions.explanation: A government can absorb a short burst of protest far more easily than a sustained one, because the cost of repression is concentrated at the moment it is used and a short protest lets the authorities wait it out. Mobilisation becomes decisive when it lasts long enough for opponents to coordinate and for the costs of suppression to outrun what the government can bear, which is why duration and organisation matter more than the anger itself. A charismatic figure can help but is not the condition, since movements outlive their leaders; and a movement does not write constitutions or suppress turnout, so the remaining options assign it tasks it does not perform.
questions.hint: Ask why a government can wait out a short protest but not a long one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain why a negotiated transition is expected to last longer
questions.stem: Explain why a transition reached by negotiation is often expected to outlast one produced by collapse, and name one cost that the bargain imposes on the order that replaces the old regime.

answer.exemplar: A negotiated transition tends to last because the outgoing elite keeps a reason to accept the result. In a pact the departing rulers receive guarantees of immunity, office or property, and the new government gains their cooperation in disarming whatever force of resistance they controlled, so the first transfer of authority happens without a contest that one side must lose outright. Collapse offers no such asset: the old leadership is defeated, often without protection, and it retains the resources and the grievance from which a counter-attack is mounted, which is why settlements reached by force are frequently reversed. The bargain is not free. It commonly leaves some of the old elite's personnel in office, insulates a few actors from prosecution, and accepts a constitution or an electoral system that suits the moment of agreement rather than the long run. The former officials then hold authority they would not otherwise have retained, and the new order begins with a debt owed to people whose interests it was meant to end. So the durability and the cost are two sides of one design.

questions.explanation: A model answer should tie durability to the departing elite's incentive to accept the result, and identify a cost such as retained officeholders, amnesty for past abuses, or a settlement written for the moment rather than the long run.
questions.hint: Ask what makes one side willing to let go of power, and what it extracts in return.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the choice of sequence between constitution and elections
questions.stem: A government must decide whether to hold elections before or after writing a constitution that limits the executive. Which claim about that sequencing choice is best supported?

options.text: Each order carries a distinct risk, and no general principle settles which to choose
Elections first is always safer, since a legislature can revise a constitution
options.misconception: asserts a universal ranking the choice does not support

options.text: A constitution first is always safer, because written words bind any successor
options.misconception: assumes a text constrains whoever inherits office from it

options.text: The order is immaterial, since each instrument binds its own authors in the same way
options.misconception: denies the sequence a difference that the two instruments' timing creates

questions.explanation: The two orders carry different and genuine risks, which is why the choice is contested. Elections first put a legislature in place that may decline to ratify the limits on the executive, so a government that intends real constraint may be unable to secure it; a constitution first fixes the rules before anyone has a mandate to change them, so the government writing it may be the one it constrains. Neither instrument binds its successors automatically, and a legislature is free to entrench or to amend a text, so the two claims that rank one order as always safer both assume a constraint that does not follow from writing or winning. The defensible position is that the sequence must be argued on the country's circumstances.
questions.hint: Ask what each instrument can and cannot achieve about the one that follows it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain the incumbent's incentive to bias a contest
questions.stem: Explain why a sitting government has an incentive to bias an election even when independent polling suggests it will probably lose, and name one cost it accepts by doing so.

answer.exemplar: The polling result is an average, and an incumbent optimising for the outcome has no reason to accept the average. Two properties of the electoral process make this concrete. First, close contests are decided by the marginal voter, and a rule that raises the cost of participation, the distance to a polling place or the effort required to obtain a missing credential has a larger effect on a party whose supporters are younger, poorer or more mobile than on a party whose supporters are already likely to turn out. The expected value of such a measure can be positive even when the party's overall support is lower, because it changes the distribution of turnout rather than the distribution of preference. Second, the information is not symmetric: the incumbent knows the rules it is writing, and the other parties must campaign under whatever rules emerge, so a measure adopted quietly is not matched in advance. The cost is that the bias becomes public. Once opponents and observers can identify the intervention, the government's own claim to a mandate is discounted, judges are asked to review measures passed to favour one side, and the possibility that a later government will reverse the same practices makes every future government a potential target. A government that expects to lose an election has, in effect, purchased a worse outcome if it loses and a less legitimate one if it wins.

questions.explanation: A model answer should link the incentive to the marginal effects on turnout and to the asymmetry of information about the rules, and should identify a cost such as lost legitimacy, judicial review, or the prospect of later reversal.

stimulus.body: Terms of a transition agreement, written for this question. Clause 1: elections are to be held on the date fixed in the annex, and any postponement requires the written consent of the guarantor's representative. Clause 2: the guarantor will recognise the result of the election, whatever it is, within seven days of the official count. Clause 3: the guarantor will not recognise any government formed otherwise than by the elected assembly. Clause 4: any dispute about the count is to be settled by a commission whose members are named in equal numbers by the outgoing government, the incoming majority and the guarantor.

questions.stem: Four clauses of a transition agreement are quoted: elections are to be held on the annexed date and any postponement needs the guarantor's written consent; the guarantor will recognise the result whatever it is within seven days of the count; the guarantor will recognise no government formed otherwise than by the elected assembly; and any dispute about the count goes to a commission whose members are named in equal numbers by the outgoing government, the incoming majority and the guarantor. Which risk does the agreement do least to remove?

options.text: A contested count, which is left to a commission that is one third interested
A challenge to the result by a defeated party, which the recognition clause answers
options.misconception: reports a live dispute where the quoted clause forecloses one

options.text: A refusal to hold the vote at all, which the consent clause forecloses
options.misconception: treats a requirement for consent as a guarantee that the vote happens

options.text: A government formed outside the assembly, which the recognition clause rules out
options.misconception: reports a live risk where the quoted clause excludes one

questions.explanation: Clauses 1 to 3 each remove a specific risk: the annex plus the consent requirement addresses the timing of the vote, and the two recognition clauses settle what happens to a result and to any government not produced by the assembly. What none of them touches is a disagreement about the count itself, and that is left to a commission on which the two sides to the dispute each hold a third of the seats. That is not fatal, because a third party breaks a tie and an agreed procedure is better than none, but it is the part of the arrangement that leaves a real interest in dispute. The contrast with clauses 2 and 3 is the point: where the text speaks, the risk is closed.
questions.hint: Look for the one subject the clauses set a procedure for rather than a rule about.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain the function of tolerated opposition
questions.stem: Some authoritarian systems allow a few legal parties to contest elections, on condition that they stay within limits the government sets. What is the strategic purpose of tolerating them?

options.text: It supplies the appearance of competition while leaving the incumbent's position secure
It gives voters a real chance to remove the incumbent at the next vote
options.misconception: reads permitted competition as though it were effective competition

options.text: It meets a constitutional court's demand for genuinely plural competition
options.misconception: invents a judicial instruction the system was said to resist

options.text: It lowers the administrative cost of holding elections each year
options.misconception: attaches a budgeting motive to a political arrangement

questions.explanation: The purpose of permitting a limited opposition is informational and presentational rather than competitive. Voters, officials and outside observers are given evidence that contests occur, which helps the government present itself as a normal electoral state, while the limits placed on what the permitted parties may do keep the incumbent's own position out of reach. The other answers each assume an effect the arrangement is designed to withhold: a genuine chance of removal, a court's demand that the system meet, and a saving on administrative cost. Toleration is a way of managing the appearance of competition, not evidence of it.
questions.hint: Ask what the government gains by allowing a contest it has made safe.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify a legislature that provides no real check
questions.stem: A legislature sits for a few months in each year, holds little debate, and votes almost always as its majority party directs. What is that body usually described as?

options.text: A rubber-stamp legislature, which leaves the effective initiative with the executive
A deliberative body, which weighs each measure carefully before deciding
options.misconception: reads infrequent debate as evidence of thorough deliberation

options.text: A two-chamber body, which must reconcile two separately elected houses
options.misconception: confuses a voting pattern with a two-chamber structure

options.text: A standing body, which by definition serves a fixed term
options.misconception: mistakes the length of a body's existence for how it votes

Nothing about the number of chambers, the length of the body's life or a general presumption of careful debate follows from that pattern, so the remaining answers attach structural descriptions to what is in fact a behavioural one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: identify the effect established by a deregistration rule

stimulus.body: Statutory extract, written for this question. Article 3: a registered party must deposit with the electoral authority a written declaration of its programme at least ninety days before any election. Article 4: the authority may deregister a party by a decision of five of its seven members where it is satisfied that the party's programme calls for a change to the form of the state. Article 5: the candidates of a deregistered party may not stand in the election concerned. Article 6: the authority must publish its reasons in a quarterly bulletin.

questions.stem: A statutory extract requires parties to file their programmes ninety days before an election, lets the electoral authority deregister a party by a decision of five of its seven members where it is satisfied the programme calls for changing the form of the state, bars the candidates of a deregistered party from standing in that election, and requires the authority to publish its reasons in a quarterly bulletin. Which effect does the extract establish?

options.text: A party can be removed from a contest before a single vote is counted
The quarterly bulletin gives the public a route to overturn a deregistration
options.misconception: describes a publication duty as a remedy against the decision

options.text: A party may be removed only if every member of the authority agrees
options.misconception: reports unanimity where the text requires five of seven

options.text: The ninety-day rule stops any party registering late in a campaign
options.misconception: turns a filing deadline into a bar on registering at all

questions.explanation: The chain in the text is deregistration, then exclusion from the ballot, and both operate before the count. Once a party is removed, its candidates cannot stand, so the exclusion happens in the absence of any votes rather than in response to them, which is what the correct answer describes. The other claims either add something the text does not provide or take something away from it. A quarterly bulletin is a duty to publish reasons, not a route to appeal, and five of seven members is a working majority rather than unanimity. The ninety-day rule sets when a programme must be deposited; it does not bar a party from registering at all.
questions.hint: Follow the text's own sequence and ask when the exclusion takes effect.

questions.topic: Two-thirds arithmetic in a large assembly
questions.learningObjective: compute a two-thirds threshold in a 193-member body
questions.stem: An assembly of 193 member states must approve a resolution on a matter its rules place in the two-thirds category. How many affirmative votes are needed, and how much more than a simple majority is that?

options.text: 129 votes, which is 32 more than the 97 a simple majority needs
97 votes, since a bare majority already reaches the two-thirds threshold
options.misconception: reports a simple majority as if it satisfied a two-thirds rule

options.text: 128 votes, because two thirds of 193 stops just short of 129
options.misconception: truncates a fractional threshold instead of rounding to a whole vote

options.text: 193 votes, because the rules require unanimity on such resolutions
options.misconception: substitutes a requirement of unanimity for the stated threshold

questions.explanation: Two thirds of 193 is 128.67, so 128 votes is not enough and the smallest workable figure is 129, which is about 66.8 percent of the assembly. A bare majority of the same body is 97, being half of 193 rounded up, and the gap between the two thresholds is therefore 32 votes. The other answers each misread the rule: 97 satisfies no two-thirds requirement, 128 falls one vote short of the fraction the text imposes, and unanimity is a different and much higher rule that the case does not state.
questions.hint: Compute two thirds of 193, then round up to a whole vote.

questions.topic: Comparing three countries on one measure
questions.learningObjective: compare profiles on a shared indicator set

stimulus.body: Assessment extract, written for this question. Three countries are assessed on the same five indicators, and a country is recorded as failing an indicator where the assessment is negative. Country X fails three indicators: judicial independence, media freedom and the impartiality of the electoral administration. Country Y fails all five. Country Z fails one, judicial independence. Country Y also fails two indicators that X and Z pass.

questions.stem: Three countries are assessed on the same five indicators. X fails three, namely judicial independence, media freedom and the impartiality of the electoral administration; Y fails all five; Z fails one, judicial independence. What is the soundest comparison among them?

options.text: Z is nearest the democratic end of this measure, and X sits between it and Y
Y belongs above X, because failing every test at least shows consistency
options.misconception: treats uniform failure as evidence of a better standing

options.text: X and Y are indistinguishable, since both defeat a court's independence
options.misconception: makes two different profiles identical on the strength of one shared item

options.text: Z is a democracy, since it passes four of the five indicators
options.misconception: declares a category from a single passing indicator and ignores the rest

questions.explanation: On a shared scale the ordering follows from how many indicators each country fails: Z fails 1 of 5, X fails 3 of 5, and Y fails 5 of 5, which is 20, 60 and 100 percent of the set. Z is therefore closest to the democratic end and X is the intermediate case, and the profile matters as well as the count, since Z's single failure is on judicial independence while X's three cover the courts, the media and the electoral administration. The other readings either reward consistency, collapse two distinct profiles because they share one item, or promote a country into a category on the strength of what it passes rather than what it fails.
questions.hint: Rank the three countries by how many of the same five indicators each fails.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain how selective benefits sustain a regime
questions.stem: Where benefits from public office, licences and contracts reach a narrow circle of recipients, what effect does that distribution have on the durability of the government dispensing it?

options.text: It ties the recipients' livelihoods to the dispenser, so they resist a change of government
It raises state revenue, because each payment is recorded as a receipt
options.misconception: recasts a political payment as an item of fiscal income

options.text: It reduces corruption, since one patron can supervise every recipient
options.misconception: reads concentrated patronage as a remedy for misconduct

options.text: It gives opposition members a reason to join the governing party
options.misconception: describes party discipline as though it were a cash payment

questions.explanation: Durability comes from a constituency with something to lose. When the benefits of office, licensing and contracting are concentrated, the small number who receive them gain materially from the government staying in power, and they are correspondingly reluctant to support an alternative. That is a structural argument about incentives, and it explains why such arrangements persist even when they are publicly criticised. Payments to recipients are not revenue for the state, a single patron does not remove the underlying corruption but is its instrument, and nothing in the distribution buys loyalty from a party opponent. The effect runs from benefit to incentive to durability.
questions.hint: Ask what a recipient would lose if the government changed.

questions.learningObjective: interpret a change in ownership of a broadcast channel
questions.stem: A government transfers the largest television channel to a company whose principal shareholder is a long-standing political ally, and the channel's nightly bulletin thereafter carries only official accounts of a contested referendum. Which inference is best supported by that sequence?

The referendum was not genuinely contested, since only official accounts appeared
options.misconception: draws a conclusion about the vote from the range of coverage

options.text: The transfer of ownership was itself decided by the referendum result
options.misconception: invents a causal link running from the vote to the transfer

options.text: The new ownership has freed the channel from commercial pressure
options.misconception: reads a change of proprietor as an absence of pressure

Nor does the case connect the vote to the transfer, which the sequence places first, and a politically connected owner is a source of pressure rather than its removal.
questions.hint: Ask which change came first, and what a change of owner would be expected to affect.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Order in which defensive measures bite
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages by which a position is made hard to overturn
questions.stem: Put these five developments in the order in which they typically take effect, as one party's position in a constitutional system is made progressively harder to overturn.

options.text: The governing party brings pressure on courts that have ruled against it
Reporting of criticism narrows to channels the party does not control
Investigations are directed at opposition parties rather than at the governing party's own
Rules governing how the count will be conducted are issued just before polling
The result is announced and the incoming government is never seated

questions.explanation: The order follows the logic of removing checks from the top down. The courts come first because they are the body able to invalidate the government's own acts, and a government that can discipline them has removed the one institution that might undo what it does. The information environment is next, since limiting the channels that carry criticism narrows what the public can learn before it votes. The targeting of investigations then reduces the opposition's ability to organise at the same time as its visibility is reduced, and only after all of that does the count itself come under control. The last stage is the consequence the whole sequence is designed to produce, so the order is A, B, C, D, E.
questions.hint: Ask which check has to be weakened before the next one can be used at all.

questions.learningObjective: identify the design of a conditional campaign grant
questions.stem: An opposition party is granted a fixed annual sum for campaign costs, on terms set by the governing majority. What is the likely design of that arrangement?

options.text: Access to public money is conditional on rules the governing party itself sets
The grant is unconditional, so every party competes on equal financial terms
options.misconception: assumes the absence of a stated penalty means the absence of a condition

options.text: The grant is withdrawn whenever the opposition leads in the polls
options.misconception: invents an automatic trigger that the stated terms do not contain

options.text: The grant is confined to election years, so spending cannot be permanent
options.misconception: substitutes a restriction on timing for a condition on the amount

questions.explanation: Where the terms of a grant are set by the party that the grant is intended to fund, equality of access is not established by the payment itself. The amount may be fixed while the conditions attached to it are variable, and conditions on how money may be spent, on reporting or on campaign timing give the government a say over the recipient's conduct that the absence of a stated penalty does not remove. That is the reason campaign funding rules are contested at all. The other answers each add a term the case does not state: no automatic withdrawal on a poll lead, no single unconditional guarantee, and a timing limit is a different constraint from a condition on the amount.
questions.hint: Ask who writes the rules attached to the money.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: explain the incumbent's calculation in tolerating opposition
questions.stem: Explain why a government that expects to win at the ballot box may still choose to permit legal opposition parties, and name one risk it accepts by doing so.

answer.exemplar: There are three reasons that bear on the calculation, and they point in different directions. The first is informational and reputational. A state that forbids parties can be described by outsiders as a closed system, which raises the cost of borrowing, of attracting investment and of being invited to the international bodies that most governments want to join, whereas a state that holds contested elections is described in different terms whatever the result. The second is about the margin of victory. An election that is competitive but lost badly looks like a rejection of the whole government, while a competitive election narrowly lost looks like an ordinary fluctuation that the winner can survive. The third is that the existence of a legal opposition gives the government somewhere to put the blame for a policy failure, and removing that target concentrates every grievance on the government itself. The risks run in the other direction. A permitted opposition can build an organisation, a funding base and a public profile while doing nothing that looks illegal, and incumbents who expect to win do not always do; a legal opposition that wins once is far harder to dislodge than one that never had a platform, and the precedent of a permitted contest can be used to argue for a further one. So the calculation is that the present benefits of appearing open outweigh the possibility that the arrangement creates its own opponent.

questions.explanation: A model answer should offer at least two of the three reasons, such as international standing, the margin of victory, or a target for blame, and should name a risk such as a built-up challenger or the precedent of tolerating further demands.
questions.hint: Ask what the government gains from being seen to allow a contest it expects to win, and what that contest lets grow.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the claim that elections are sufficient for democracy
questions.stem: A government argues that regular competitive elections are by themselves sufficient for a state to count as a democracy. Which consideration most seriously weakens that claim?

options.text: Elections can be genuinely competitive while the surrounding institutions cannot check the winner
Competitive elections usually produce a single party, so the claim needs qualifying
options.misconception: answers a claim about sufficiency with one about party systems

options.text: Elections are contested in almost no country, so the argument never applies
options.misconception: dismisses the electoral criterion the argument relies on

options.text: Turnout is higher where elections are contested, so democracy should be measured by voting
options.misconception: accepts a correlation about turnout as a settlement of a design question

questions.explanation: Sufficiency is a strong claim, and the strongest objection is that it treats one element of a system as though it delivered the whole. Elections decide who holds office, and they do so at one moment, while the ability of a government to be restrained depends on institutions that operate continuously: a legislature that can scrutinise, a court that can invalidate, an administration that is answerable. A state may therefore hold competitive elections at regular intervals and still be governed by a winner unconstrained between them, which is a live difficulty rather than a technicality, since a vote that cannot remove a government has lost the feature that made it worth holding. The other options either attack a claim the government has not made or accept a correlation as an answer.
questions.hint: Ask what an election can decide, and what it cannot decide between one vote and the next.

questions.topic: A court with no adverse rulings
questions.learningObjective: interpret a court's record of never invalidating executive acts
questions.stem: A constitutional court has never once invalidated an executive measure, and its judgments are described by observers as careful and well argued. What does that record support?

options.text: On the cases it has heard, the court is not operating as a check on the executive
The executive has always complied, so the court has had nothing to strike down
options.misconception: takes compliance for granted instead of testing for it

options.text: The court has been given a narrower jurisdiction than the constitution allows
options.misconception: invents a change in jurisdiction to account for a pattern of outcomes

options.text: The constitution gives the executive a right to review each of the judgments
options.misconception: asserts a review power the case nowhere mentions

questions.explanation: A court's function in a system of checks includes striking down acts it considers unlawful, so a record of no invalidation across every case it has heard is evidence about the court's operation rather than about the executive's conduct. The two explanations are hard to separate on the record alone, but they are not equally available, because an executive that always complies leaves nothing for a court to test, whereas a court that never tests leaves nothing to observe. The quality of the reasoning is a separate matter and does not supply the missing check. Nor does the case report a narrower jurisdiction or a power of executive review, so those explanations have nothing to rest on.
questions.hint: Ask what a check has to be observed doing before we can count it as working.

questions.learningObjective: identify what conditional access leaves unobserved
questions.stem: Observer missions are admitted to monitor elections only where the host government agrees to admit them. What does that condition leave outside the coverage of the missions?

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: distinguish constitutional from nominal federalism
questions.stem: Two states both describe themselves as federal. The first has a constitution reserving listed powers to its constituent units and requiring their consent for any change to them; the second is called a federation in law while the centre may legislate on any subject. What follows from the contrast?

options.text: One label is covering two arrangements, and the constitutional text settles which is which
The second state is a federation in name only, a settled legal conclusion
options.misconception: presents a contested characterisation as though it were a ruling

options.text: The first state is unitary, since a written constitution cannot make a federation
options.misconception: denies the reserved-powers arrangement the text sets out

options.text: Neither state is federal, because a federation needs a single founding act
options.misconception: imposes on both cases a requirement for one kind of founding instrument

questions.explanation: The two states differ in whether the constituent units have powers the centre cannot touch, and that difference is settled by the constitution rather than by a preference about naming. Where powers are reserved and their alteration requires the consent of the units, the arrangement is federal in the constitutional sense; where the centre may legislate on any subject, whatever the description, the units hold whatever the centre grants. The second answer asserts a conclusion that in practice is often contested rather than settled, which is why the text is the right place to look. The last answer adds a requirement about how a federation must be created, which neither constitution addresses.
questions.hint: Ask whether the centre can legislate on subjects the units have reserved to themselves.

questions.learningObjective: select the correct method for combining subgroup shares
questions.stem: First stage: a survey finds a party's support at 30 percent among men and 52 percent among women, and women are 70 percent of the electorate. Second stage: which calculation is required before the overall figure can be stated consistently with those two?

options.text: Weighting the two subgroup shares by the size of each group in the electorate
Averaging the two shares, which treats the electorate as split down the middle
options.misconception: averages two shares resting on very differently sized groups

options.text: Adding the two shares, which counts every respondent as though counted twice
options.misconception: sums percentages drawn from overlapping groups

options.text: Taking the larger of the two shares as the overall result
options.misconception: substitutes one group's share for the electorate as a whole

questions.explanation: An overall share is a weighted average of the subgroup shares, and the weights are the sizes of the groups. With men at 30 percent of a body that is 30 percent male, and women at 52 percent of a body that is 70 percent female, the overall figure is 9 plus 36.4, or 45.4 percent. The other methods produce different numbers for the wrong reasons: a simple average of 30 and 52 gives 41, which would only be right if the two groups were the same size, and they are not; adding the two gives 82, which counts every respondent twice; and taking the larger share reports women alone as though they were the electorate.
questions.hint: Ask how large each group is in the body you are trying to describe.

questions.learningObjective: identify the effect of a reserved power on central reform

stimulus.body: Programme review, written for this question. A government elected four years ago promised to build 40 clinics. The review records that 31 were completed and opened, 5 were begun and then abandoned, and 4 were never started. It also records that the responsible ministry costed each clinic at 3 million and that the total amount appropriated for the programme over the four years was 120 million.

questions.stem: A government promised 40 clinics. A review records 31 completed and opened, 5 begun and then abandoned, and 4 never started. The ministry costed each clinic at 3 million, and total appropriations for the programme over the four years came to 120 million. What does the review show about delivery and about the money?

options.text: Close to four fifths of the clinics opened, and the appropriation matched the estimate for all forty
Under one clinic in ten opened, so the programme very largely failed
options.misconception: reads the incomplete remainder as if it were the whole programme

options.text: The appropriation could fund the promised clinics twice over, so the shortfall was avoidable
options.misconception: divides the appropriation by the cost of one clinic and doubles the promise

options.text: Each opened clinic cost the whole 120 million, so costs ran far beyond the estimate
options.misconception: assigns the entire four-year appropriation to a single unit

questions.explanation: Thirty-one of forty clinics is 77.5 percent, which is short of four fifths by a small margin and plainly not the collapse the second answer describes. On the money, forty clinics at 3 million each would cost 120 million, and 120 million was appropriated, so the appropriation matched the estimate for the full programme rather than exceeding or falling short of it; the 93 million spent on opened clinics leaves 27 million for the nine that were begun or not started. That last figure is the more interesting one, since it shows money remaining unspent on work that was never finished, but the review as written supports the comparison the correct answer makes.
questions.hint: Compare 31 with 40, and compare 40 clinics at the stated cost with the appropriation.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: What a court's adverse ruling demonstrates
questions.learningObjective: explain why an adverse ruling is the test of a check
questions.stem: A newly consolidated democracy is described as one whose courts have begun to rule against governments that have been in office. Why does the account treat that development as significant?

options.text: A check is only observed working when it produces an outcome someone in power dislikes
The courts have become independent of the constitution they were given
options.misconception: treats independence as freedom from the founding text

options.text: Policy-making has passed from the government into the hands of the judges
options.misconception: reverses which branch is described as taking over the deciding role

options.text: Elections have stopped deciding who holds office in the country
options.misconception: moves the significance from the courts to the electoral process

questions.explanation: A check cannot be observed in the speeches of its members, only in what it does when it is unwelcome, which is why an adverse ruling is the evidence that matters. A court that never contradicts a government may be well argued, well paid and entirely inert, and the observer cannot tell those possibilities apart without a case in which the ruling went the other way. Independence here means independence from the government, not from the constitution the court is applying, so the first distractor inverts the term. Nor does the development transfer policy-making to the courts or reduce elections to irrelevance; it is a statement about one institution beginning to function as a check.
questions.hint: Ask how anyone could tell a working check from an idle one without a case that was decided against the government.
